at the time of the sacrifice. At the time the sacrifice is offered.
to the men of the ancestral house who offer on that day. The priests appointed over the Temple service on that day (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:11).
the holy things of the Temple. The priestly gifts given in the Temple (see Hilchot Bikkurim 1:10).
a meal-offering against a meal-offering. One priest receives a whole meal-offering and in return the other receives another meal-offering, and they do not divide the meal-offerings themselves.
and likewise a woman and an androgynos. Who may eat lesser sacrifices (above halakhot 4-6, 9).
but a blemished priest... divides and eats. See also Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 6:12.
whether permanent or transient. For the details of the types of blemishes, see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash chapter 8.
and the High Priest eats not by division but takes whatever he wishes. And takes his portion first (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:12).

a tevul yom. An impure person who immersed; as long as the sun has not set on him he is in a mild state of impurity and forbidden to eat terumah and sacred offerings (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:1-2).

and one lacking atonement. A zav, a zavah, a woman after childbirth and a leper who have become pure of their impurity, and are forbidden to eat sacred offerings until they bring a sacrifice to complete their purification process (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1).

and an onen on the day of burial. One whose relative died is forbidden to serve and to eat sacred offerings on the day of burial, and at night afterward it is permitted (provided the burial was not on the day of death, Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 2:9-10).
who serves but does not eat, as we have explained. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 2:8.
except a blemished priest, for it is specified in the Torah. See above halakhah 17.
whoever has no share in the meat has no share in the skins. The skins of most holy offerings that the priests acquire (above 5:19).

even if he was impure at the time of the sprinkling of blood and pure at the time of the burning of the fats. For example, the fats were burned at night after his sun had set, or one lacking atonement brought his sacrifice between the sprinkling and the burning.

the matter is in doubt whether he divides or does not divide. The doubt is whether it suffices that he be pure at the time of the services, or he must be pure from the beginning of the services to their end.

therefore if he seized, it is not taken from his hand. Because of the doubt he cannot claim a share in the sacrifice, and they do not give him a share. But if he took himself, what he took cannot be taken from him since perhaps it is due to him (for this principle see also Hilchot Bechorot 2:6, Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 9:11 and elsewhere).

a communal sacrifice that comes in impurity, even though the impure offer it. When most of the congregation (or the service vessels or the priests) are impure, the impure are permitted to offer sacrifices whose time is fixed (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:9-10; this speaks of a case where the meat did not become impure, see Radbaz and Arukh HaShulchan 82:19).
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
for this is a warning against eating the flesh of the burnt-offering. A warning not to eat. And from this verse they also learned the warning about misuse of sacred things (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:3).
its libations. The meal-offering of libations that comes with the burnt-offering (above 2:1-2).
all five join to make an olive's bulk. For liability to lashes if he ate them (and likewise for misuse if he benefited from them, Commentary on the Mishnah, Me'ilah 4:2).
the sacrificial fats. See above 1:18.
entirely to the altar. All of them are burned on the altar.
in the priests' meal-offering. The meal-offerings brought by priests are burned on the altar, and are not eaten like other meal-offerings (below 12:9).
from the flesh of the sin-offerings that are burned. Above 1:16.

before the sprinkling of the blood he is flogged. Even after the sprinkling of the blood one may not eat of the meat until the sacrificial fats are burned (above 9:11, but one is not flogged for this, Mishneh LaMelekh).
whether lesser or more stringent. Lesser sacrifices and most holy offerings.
and the bread. That comes with the thanksgiving-offering (above 9:17-18).
outside the Temple court. Above 10:3.
outside Jerusalem. Above 10:5.
and the same is true of the flesh of a sin-offering and guilt-offering or the remainders of meal-offerings. Their prohibition is equal.
outside its partition. Outside the boundary of the place where it is permitted to eat it.
as we have explained in Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot. 5:9.
flesh of offerings of lesser holiness entered the Sanctuary. And all the more so the flesh of most holy offerings (see above, 10:3).
from a bird sin offering. A bird sin offering is not slaughtered but pinched, and its flesh is eaten by the priests in the courtyard like the flesh of an animal sin offering (above, 7:6-7).
carcass. An animal or bird that died without slaughter.
for every pinched bird is a carcass. For it was not slaughtered.
and when it was permitted. The eating of the bird sin offering.

two prohibitions that come as one, as we have explained. When two prohibitions take effect at the same time, prohibition falls upon prohibition and one is flogged twice for one act (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:8).
and the meal offerings that come on their own. Apart from the meal offering of libations mentioned above, chapter 2.
fine wheat flour. Coarse flour, sifted of waste and of fine flour (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:11-12).
from the meal offering of a suspected adulteress. Which is offered at the time the suspected adulteress is given to drink (Hilchot Sotah 3:12).
and the omer of waving. The omer meal offering (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 7:11-12).
for they are of barley. The meal offering of a suspected adulteress is of barley flour and the omer meal offering is of barley fine flour.
the omer of waving, and it is offered on the altar, as will be explained. Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 7:3-12.
and the two loaves that are brought on the day of Atzeret. On the festival of Shavuot (ibid. 8:1-10).
and these are called a meal offering and are not offered on the altar. The two loaves are considered a meal offering even though they are not offered on the altar but are eaten by the priests.
the showbread that is made every Shabbat... as will be explained. There, chapter 5.

a sinner's meal offering, and it is a meal offering that a poor person offers when he becomes obligated in a sin offering and his means do not suffice. A poor person who cannot bring an animal or two birds for a burnt-or-sliding-scale sin offering brings a meal offering (Hilchot Shegagot 10:4).
the meal offering of a suspected adulteress, which is the meal offering of jealousies, whose procedures have already been explained. Hilchot Sotah 3:12-15.
the meal offering that every priest offers first when he enters the service. The first time he begins to serve in the Temple (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:16).
for he offers it with his own hand. The priest offers it himself.
the meal offering that the High Priest offers every day. Half in the morning and half between the evenings (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:18; for the manner of its preparation see below, 13:2-4).

a meal offering of fine flour... the pan... the frying pan... oven-baked loaves... oven-baked wafers. Five kinds of meal offerings that differ from one another in the manner of their preparation (below, 13:5-9), and which come as a freewill offering at the person's own wish.
as a vow and as a freewill offering. Below, 14:4.
from an isaron. A tenth of an ephah (about two liters).
and the least of it is indispensable for all of it. If he brought a meal offering of less than an isaron, the meal offering is invalid.
he may volunteer or vow of them whatever he wishes. But he must bring whole isarons (below, 17:10).
bringing near in the west opposite the tip of the southwestern corner. They bring the meal offering near the southwestern corner of the altar, at its lower part (above, 7:10).
waving. Lifting the meal offering up, down, and to the sides (above, 9:7).
for both of them require waving and bringing near. Waving and then bringing near (above, 9:16).
require oil. Which they would put on the meal offering at one of the stages of its preparation (depending on the type of meal offering - see below, chapter 13).
and frankincense. Grains of frankincense that they would put on top of the meal offering (for its identification see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 2:4).
log. About three hundred cc.
and a handful. What fits in the hand when he closes his fingers over it (the manner and measure of taking the handful are explained below, 13:13-14).
for one does not bring more than sixty in one vessel, as will be explained. Below, 17:6.
he put and offered. Oil and frankincense on the meal offering of jealousies or on a sinner's meal offering.
he is flogged for the oil by itself and for the frankincense by itself. He transgresses two prohibitions and is liable for two floggings.

he neither transgresses nor disqualified. But when he put oil or frankincense on the meal offering itself in a way that they cannot be gathered, the meal offering is disqualified (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 11:10).
the meal offering of inauguration and the griddle cakes add oil to each of them. A greater amount of oil.
as will be explained. Below, 13:2.
the priestess. The unmarried daughter of a priest or one who married an Israelite (and the law of one married to a priest is explained below, halakhah 12).
offspring that were mixed up. Where one is a priest and the other an Israelite, and it is not known which is which.

a handful is taken as for an Israelite's meal offering. In a priest's meal offering the entire meal offering is burned, and in an Israelite's meal offering only the handful is burned, and therefore the handful must be burned in any case.
and it is not eaten like a priests' meal offering. Lest it is a priest, and it is forbidden to eat his meal offering.
and the remainders are scattered at the ash-place. Which was east of the ramp, and into which they also threw the ashes of the removal of the ashes (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 2:12).
because of the husband's share. The priest husband has a connection to the woman's meal offering, and a priest's meal offering is burned.
the handful is offered by itself and the remainders are scattered at the ash-place. See also Hilchot Sotah 4:15.
and they sanctify a meal offering. Below, 13:12.
in a vessel that is on the ground. And it is not necessary that the vessel be in the hands.
and they do not sanctify the handful in a vessel that is on the ground. After taking the handful, they put the handful into a service vessel, which sanctifies it for burning on the altar (ibid.).
and from when may the remainders be eaten. The remainders of the meal offering, by the priests.
from when the fire takes hold. When the fire has caught.
that are offered on the altar. But the two loaves, which are not offered on the altar, become leavened (above, halakhah 3).
matzah. They do not go through a process of leavening and rising.
even though it is permitted to eat them in any food. Above, 10:10.
and honey. Even though there is a special prohibition against burning it on the altar (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:1).
even their portion. The remainders of the meal offerings, the priests' portion.
and one who leavens after one who leavens. For example, the dough was slightly leavened and another came and added leaven to it, causing it to become more leavened (Likkutei Halachot, Menachot 56b).
he kneaded it. He mixed flour and water.

he arranged it. Some read "he stretched it," and the meaning is that he softened and worked the dough (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 5:2; and it seems that this is also its meaning according to the reading we have, see the note of R. Y. Shilat in the Rambam Meduyak).
he pinched it off. He cut pieces of dough in order to make them into loaves (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 5:2).
leaven. Sour dough made from water and flour, used to cause other dough to rise.
he seasoned the remainders with nigella or sesame and any spices and oils, valid. For these spices do not cause leavening (Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 5:20).

except that it is called seasoned matzah. And one should not do so with the matzah of the first day of Passover (for then the matzah must be "bread of affliction" - see Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 5:20), but with regard to meal offerings there is no problem with this.
he leavened it when it was valid and it went outside. And it was disqualified by this going out (above, 11:6).
and he leavened it again after it was disqualified by going out, he is not flogged. For the second leavening (Rik"v), since it was done to a disqualified meal offering.
he leavened it on top of the altar. Before burning it on the fire.
for if he mixed it with water, it was disqualified before it could become leavened. For the meal offering of libations is fine flour mixed with oil, with nothing added.
they are fruit juices and do not cause leavening. Juice that comes out of fruit cannot cause dough to leaven without water (Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 5:2).
they rinse. They mix them with water to clean them of the bran.
lest they leaven. If they stay after rinsing (Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 5:7).

for outside they rinse them and not everyone is zealous to guard them. The preparation of the fine flour for meal offerings was done outside the Temple (below, halakhah 23), and there is concern that this would not be done with zeal and care to prevent leavening.
for the community. The court appointed over the communal offerings.
are zealous. They are meticulous about the commandments (for this principle see Hilchot Shofar 2:9).

they are kneaded with lukewarm water and he guards them so they do not leaven etc.. The heat of the water hastens leavening, and in order to prevent leavening of Passover matzah one must use completely cold water (Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 5:11). Inside the Temple they would knead with lukewarm water, since work in the Temple is done with zeal and care.
the men of the Presence are zealous. See also Hilchot Shabbat 3:20.

and in the place where they cook most holy offerings, there they bake meal offerings. Inside the courtyard, for the flesh of most holy offerings that went out is disqualified (Kesef Mishneh, and some say there was a special place for baking them inside the courtyard, Aruch HaShulchan 85:23).
all the meal offerings etc.. Except for the showbread and the two loaves, whose kneading and arranging are outside and baking inside (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 5:7, 8:7).
and sifting them. Sieving them.
outside. Outside the courtyard (see also below, 13:12).
and kneading them and arranging them. Mixing in the water, and softening the dough.
by a non-priest. An Israelite who is not a priest.
until they come to the house of taking the handful. Until the taking of the handful and the services after it, which are done only by a priest.
and the pan and the frying pan. In which they fried the meal offerings (see below, 13:7).
of the service vessels, and they sanctify. Of the vessels designated for the Temple service, and therefore they sanctified the meal offering that was placed in them.

and the oven of the Temple was of metal. The oven in which they baked the meal offerings was made of metal, and was considered one of the service vessels of the Temple (Babylonian Talmud, Zevachim 96a).
the griddle cakes of the High Priest. The griddle-cake meal offering that the High Priest offers every day, half in the morning and half between the evenings (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:18).

he brings a whole isaron etc.. They bring a tenth of an ephah of fine flour and sanctify it in the isaron measure in the Temple, and afterward they divide the isaron into two with the half-isaron measure in the Temple (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:16).
three logs. About nine hundred cc.

to add oil to it like the libations of a lamb. In all meal offerings they would put a log of oil for each isaron (above, 12:7). For the griddle-cake meal offering of the High Priest they increased the measure of oil, and put into it an amount equal to the oil of the libation meal offering of a lamb (above, 2:4).
and he soaks it in boiling water. He pours boiling water over it.
and they were made one by one. He would mix the fine flour of each loaf with its oil and arrange it for baking separately.
in the quarter-log in the Temple. In the measuring vessel of a quarter-log that was in the Temple (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:17).
and he bakes the loaf a little. In the oven, after mixing with part of the oil, soaking, and kneading.
and he does not cook it much. He does not bake it much before frying (Kesef Mishneh and others, and compare above, 9:19).
tufinei. And it is expounded: "bake it, please."
by estimation. He divides the loaves approximately.
so that he may offer half in the morning and half in the evening. Half of each loaf in the morning and half in the evening.

and he takes the halves and folds each one into two and breaks it etc.. They would fold the halves of the loaves, and afterward break them into small pieces, each one of which was folded in two (Lechem Mishneh).

and if it was an inauguration meal offering etc.. In this way they also prepare and offer the inauguration meal offering that every priest offers on the day he enters the service and the High Priest on the day of his appointment (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:16). However, the loaves of the inauguration meal offering are not divided, but are offered all at once.

and both are entirely burned for the fires. The meal offering of the High Priest and the inauguration meal offering are not eaten but burned on the altar (like other priests' meal offerings, above, 12:9).
and the oil fit for it. A log for each isaron.
and he poured into it. He pours on it.
the whole is a log to an isaron. And they divide the log of oil into the placing before the fine flour, the mixing, and the pouring.
and afterward he kneaded it with lukewarm water. As above, 12:21.
and he breaks it into pieces. As explained below, halakhah 10.
a frying pan has a rim. Sides (like a modern frying pan).
for it has a rim and it does not run out. The dough does not flow out of the frying pan.
and a pan has no rim. A flat metal sheet without sides.
and the dough that is baked in it is hard etc.. They make it hard so that it does not spill off the sides of the pan.
if loaves... and if wafers. He may become obligated to bring two kinds of oven-baked meal offering: loaves or wafers.
and he breaks. See below, halakhah 10.
he mixes the fine flour with oil. With all of the oil of the meal offering.
he kneads the fine flour with lukewarm water. Without oil.
and he anoints the wafers with oil. He spreads the oil on the wafers until it is finished.
he folds the loaf in two and the two into four and separates. He folds the meal offering twice (into four layers) and separates the folds.
and if the meal offering was of male priests etc.. The meal offering of priests (from which no handful is taken) is not divided into pieces, but is folded and the folds are left connected.
and he breaks. After he folded and separated (and in the meal offering of priests he folded without separating), he breaks the folds into small pieces the size of an olive's bulk.
he did not bring near. Above, 12:6.

only as a commandment. In the first instance (but the pouring is indispensable - Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 18a; and likewise the salting of the handful is indispensable - Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:12).
in baskets. Baskets.
a vessel that is fit to be a service vessel. One fit to be among the vessels used for holy service in the Temple, a vessel made of metal (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 1:18).
and if it was a meal offering of fine flour, he puts it into a service vessel. As it is, without preparation.
and sanctifies it in a service vessel. By this placing the fine flour of the meal offering is sanctified.
he bakes it there in the Temple. Above, 12:23.
and breaks as we have explained. Above, halakhah 10.
and puts on it its oil and its frankincense. On the fine flour or on the pieces of the baked meal offerings.
and brings it near at the southwestern corner opposite the tip of the corner. The priest brings the vessel containing the meal offering near the southwestern corner of the altar (above, 12:6).

and it suffices. He does not need to touch the fine flour of the meal offering itself to the altar, but it is enough to touch the vessel in which the meal offering is held (Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 14b).
from the place where its oil is abundant. The place in the meal offering where there is a lot of oil.
and salts it. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:11-12.
and puts it on the fires from a service vessel. He throws the meal offering onto the altar fire from the vessel.
and if it is a priests' meal offering. Which is burned entirely on the altar (above, 12:9).

in the way that anyone takes a handful, he extends the palm of his hand and takes a handful. He plunges the palm of his hand into the vessel in which the meal offering is (with the back of his hand upward), and gathers a handful from it by folding all his fingers into his palm.
he took a handful with the tips of his fingers. He inserted only the tips of his fingers into the meal offering and with them gathered the handful into his palm.
from the sides. He brought the handful into his palm from the side using the thumb, and not by folding the fingers.

he added to the handful, for example, he spread his fingers and took a handful. He did not hold his fingers together, and the grains or crumbs between his fingers were added to the amount of the handful.
and part of the handful is indispensable for all of it. If a little is lacking from the measure of the handful, it is invalid.

and the handful and the frankincense are indispensable to one another. One does not fulfill the obligation by burning the handful without the frankincense or by burning the frankincense without the handful.
and part of the oil is indispensable for all of it. If a little is lacking from the measure of the oil, the meal offering is invalid.
there is no less than a log to an isaron, as we have explained. Above, 12:7.
from the five kinds of meal offerings that come as a vow and freewill offering. Above, 13:5-8.
a meal offering of the libation meal offerings by itself. Although the libation meal offering (fine flour mixed with oil) comes with the sacrifice (above, 2:2), he may bring it on its own.
from which of the three kinds of libation meal offering we have explained. The libations for sheep, ram, and cattle (above, 2:4).
and he volunteers or vows wine by itself. For pouring on the altar without a sacrifice (below, 16:14).
oil by itself. And he offers a handful of it to the altar and the rest is eaten by the priests (ibid.).
frankincense by itself. And all of it is offered on the altar (ibid.).
because they are like a sacrifice. See also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 6:9.
two who volunteer or vow one sacrifice. See also above, 3:1.
one peridah of turtledoves or young pigeons. One single unit, one turtledove or one young pigeon.
words of tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
these bring it. Although both of them inherited it, it is not considered a meal offering brought in partnership.
what is a vow etc.. See also Hilchot Nedarim 1:2.

what is a vow and what is a freewill offering etc.. A vow obligation refers to the person who vows, who must bring a certain thing (an animal for offering or a certain sum of money) to the Temple. A freewill obligation refers to a specific animal or object, which he consecrates or designates for offering or for the needs of the Temple.
the price of this animal is upon me as a burnt offering. The obligation rests on the person and relates to him ("upon me"), and therefore it is a vow (see below, halakhah 6).
the price of this animal is a burnt offering. The obligation relates to the price of the animal and not to the person, and therefore it is a freewill offering.
and the price of this house is upon me as an offering. I must bring its value for Temple maintenance.
and the ox died and the house fell, he must pay. For this obligation is a vow (above, halakhah 4).

behold I take upon myself a burnt offering on condition that I not be liable for its responsibility etc.. He undertook to bring an offering in the language of a vow, and stipulated that after he separates the animal for the offering, he would not be liable for its responsibility if it dies.
we have already explained. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 9:14.

and he offered it in this house, he did not fulfill. Even though this house is not a house of idolatry, it is impossible to offer sacrifices in it, and therefore he did not fulfill his obligation of offering in this house.

that I will offer it in this house etc.. He undertook to bring an offering that would be offered outside the Temple. Since it is impossible to offer outside the Temple, the meaning of his condition is that he vowed to consecrate a burnt offering without taking responsibility for it, so that he would be able to offer it in the Temple or to kill it outside. Therefore when he offered it not in the Temple, he fulfilled his vow (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 13:10).
and is punishable by karet for offering it up outside. Like one who offers a sacrifice outside the Temple (below, 18:2).

on condition that I shave in this house. When a nazirite completes the days of his nazirite period, he must shave the hair of his head and bring offerings to the Temple (Hilchot Nezirut 8:1-2). These offerings are called "the shaving of nazirite status" (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 13:10), and if he took nazirite status upon himself on condition that he bring his offerings to this house, this is not a taking on of nazirite status but an unspecified undertaking not to drink wine and the like.

behold this is a sin offering or a guilt offering, he said nothing. Even if he is obligated in a sin offering or a guilt offering, since he did not separate it for a particular sin, the consecration does not take effect (Tosefta, Temurah 3:12, Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 6a).
one who says, "The offering of this leper or this woman who gave birth is upon me" etc.. A person took upon himself to bring for them the offerings that they are obligated in.

if that leper or woman who gave birth were poor, the one who vowed brings a poor person's offering etc.. The offerings of the leper or the woman who gave birth vary according to the financial situation of the person (Hilchot Shegagot 10:2-3), and this is determined by the person who is obligated in the offering, even if the one who vowed is himself poor (however, if the one who vowed is rich, he must bring a rich person's offering even though the woman who gave birth or the leper are poor - Kesef Mishneh and Rik"v based on Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 5:11).
he lets him offer them on his behalf. For him.
and he is atoned for. The person who was obligated in the offering was released by the offering of the one who offered.

behold I take upon myself like the vows of the wicked, whose vows are nazirite, offering, and oath, he is liable for all of them. When he obligated himself to something and said that if he transgresses his words it shall be upon him "like the vows of the wicked, whose vows are nazirite, offering, and oath," since the wicked are accustomed to vow and swear in a time of anger and the like, and if he transgressed his words he is obligated to bring an offering that comes by vow (a burnt offering or peace offering, Meiri, Nedarim 2a), and he becomes a nazirite, and he transgressed the prohibition of an oath (Hilchot Nedarim 1:25-26; and if he said only "like the vows of the wicked be upon me" he is liable for an offering only, ibid.).

like the vows of the righteous, he is not liable for anything. The righteous do not act rashly and carelessly out of anger, and therefore they do not obligate themselves by a vow because one who vows is responsible for it, and through this they might come to transgress "you shall not delay" (ibid., Commentary on the Mishnah, Nedarim 1:1).

like the freewill offerings of the righteous, he has vowed nazirite and offering. If he continued to say "whose freewill offerings are nazirite and offering" (Hilchot Nedarim there), for the way of the righteous is to bring the offering to the courtyard and pledge it there (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nedarim 1:1). Therefore when he said "like the freewill offerings of the righteous," he obligated himself in what he said.
and all substitutes for "offering" are like "offering". Taking upon oneself a vow to bring an offering, said in a garbled form common in that place, obligates (ibid. 1:16-17).
his mouth and his heart. His speech and his intention.
one who intended to say "behold I take upon myself a burnt offering" and said "peace offerings". See also Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:3.
he intended to vow a burnt offering and said "offering"... his words stand. He is obligated to bring a burnt offering.
for a burnt offering is an offering. A burnt offering is a kind of offering, and therefore there is no contradiction between his mouth and his heart.
and herem is consecration. Consecrating his property in the language of herem is consecration for Temple maintenance or for the priests (Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 6:1).
in vows and freewill offerings he does not need to utter with his lips. In contrast to vows and oaths of prohibition (Hilchot Nedarim 2:2, Hilchot Shevuot 2:10).
he resolved in his heart. He decided finally.
on the festival he first encounters. The first festival after the vow.
and one is not flogged for this negative commandment because it has no act. For one is flogged for a transgression only if it involves an actual act (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1-2).
from valuations and pledges. Financial obligations to the Temple (Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 1:10, and see also there halakhah 1).
and tithes. That he must separate from his produce.
and gifts to the poor. Gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner (and regarding charity see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:1).
and he redeemed it on another animal. He redeemed the blemished consecrated animal with another animal, and thereby the second animal became consecrated in its place (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:10).
an heir does not transgress "you shall not delay". For a vow that his father vowed, although he must bring it (above, 3:9).

and the court is commanded to make him do it immediately, until he offers his offerings on the first festival he encounters. The court is commanded to compel him ("make him do it") to bring the offerings he vowed before the first festival passes, so that he not transgress a positive commandment (Rik"v; and some explained that immediately after three festivals have passed over him they compel him to offer on the next festival - Aruch HaShulchan 91:11).
even though it says "of his own will". And from this it follows that the offering must come from the person's own will.

they compel him until he says, "I want to". And this is not compulsion against his will, but when he says "I want to," his true will is revealed, which was subject to his evil inclination and was freed by the compulsion of the court (see Hilchot Gerushin 2:20).
they take pledges from them. They take a pledge from them until they offer (see Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 3:14).
that withhold atonement. Bringing the offering withholds their atonement.

except for a nazirite's sin offering, since it does not prevent him from drinking wine. After they throw the blood of one of the offerings the nazirite brings on the day of his purity, he is permitted to drink wine (Hilchot Nezirut 8:5).
one who says. About a pregnant animal.
its offspring. The fetus she will give birth to.

the offspring of this one is a burnt offering and she is a peace offering, his words stand. One who consecrates the offspring does not consecrate its mother, and therefore he can afterward consecrate her with a different sanctity.

she is a peace offering and her offspring is a burnt offering, if he intended this, his words stand. If when he consecrated the animal he intended that the offspring would not be consecrated with its mother but with a different sanctity, his words stand.

and if after he resolved in his heart and uttered with his lips that she would be a peace offering etc.. If at the time of consecrating the mother he did not intend to consecrate the offspring with another sanctity, the offspring was consecrated together with its mother and became a peace offering, and he cannot again consecrate it as a burnt offering.

within the time of speech. The amount of time needed to say "Peace to you, Rabbi" (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17). Ordinarily, retracting within the time of speech cancels the previous statement, but here this rule does not apply (see also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 2:9).
it shall be sold to those obligated in burnt offerings. Who will offer it.
except for the price of that limb. For its price is consecrated.

and this is provided that this one who is obligated in a burnt offering who bought it vowed a burnt offering for fixed money. Since the leg of the animal was consecrated by the earlier owner, the buyer cannot fulfill his obligation to bring a burnt offering with it (for he is like one who consecrates an animal without a leg). However, when his obligation was fixed at a specific sum, and the price of the animal without the leg equals this sum (or is higher), he fulfills his obligation with this animal, even though the sanctity of its leg is from the first one's consecration.
for the soul depends on it. For the animal's life depends on it.
he consecrated one limb of a bird. On which the soul depends (Kesef Mishneh; and Rik"v explained that the doubt is also regarding a limb on which the soul does not depend).
it is consecrated and not offered. The animal is consecrated with the sanctity of a burnt offering and the sanctity of a peace offering and it is impossible to offer it.
until it has a blemish and is sold. After it has a blemish they redeem it, and through this it becomes unconsecrated and its price is consecrated (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:10).
it shall die, as will be explained regarding sin offerings that die. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1; and there the manner of putting them to death is explained.
and he bought the other half. He bought the second half from the partner.
even though it was rejected from the start when he consecrated its half. At the beginning, when he consecrated the first half, it was impossible to offer the animal at all.

what was rejected from the start is not rejected, even though it is the sanctity of value. There is a rule regarding sacred things (whether the sanctity of the body or the sanctity of value) that something that was fit for offering and was rejected because of a particular disqualification is disqualified entirely even if the cause of the disqualification no longer exists ("what was fit and was rejected does not become fit again" - see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:6). However, when the thing was not fit for offering from the beginning, when it becomes fit it is offered ("what was rejected from the start is not rejected"; see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 3:22-24 and the explanation there).

since it is a living creature, living creatures are not rejected. It seems there is another reason here for the stated law: that the rule "what was fit and was rejected does not become fit again" does not apply to living creatures while they are alive. Therefore when he again consecrated the other half and the animal became fit, he can offer it (for this rule see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin there, Hilchot Shegagot 3:8 and others).

and makes a substitute. One who says of an unconsecrated animal that it shall be a substitute for a consecrated animal: the consecrated animal remains in its sanctity and in addition sanctity takes hold of the substituted animal (Hilchot Temurah 1:1). When one of the partners made a substitution, the substitute is not consecrated (ibid.), but after he bought the share of his fellow, the substitute becomes consecrated.
if it was fit to be offered as a burnt offering. An unblemished male.
the sanctity of the body took effect. Even in a case where he consecrated it for its value, the sanctity of the body for the altar takes hold of it (see also Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 5:14).

it shall be sold. After it has a blemish (Commentary on the Mishnah, Temurah 3:3, Kesef Mishneh; and see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:16; and some wrote that it is sold even without a blemish, Rik"v).

he said nothing, as we have explained in the laws of things forbidden for the altar. 3:10 (and there it implies that when he consecrated them for the altar the sanctity of the body did not take effect but the sanctity of value - see there in the explanation. And it is possible that the reference here to the laws of things forbidden for the altar refers to the case mentioned shortly after, "these are for a burnt offering," in which case the sanctity of value takes effect on the animal and it is sold and he brings a burnt offering with its proceeds).

these are for a burnt offering, they shall be sold and he shall bring a burnt offering with their proceeds. Since this concerns things forbidden for the altar on which no sanctity takes effect, his words must be explained as meaning that he intended to consecrate their value for a burnt offering (Radbaz).

his words stand. And he sells the animal and brings with its proceeds as he vowed: within thirty days a burnt offering and after thirty days a peace offering (and although above, halakhah 5, it was explained that when he consecrated an animal for its value and it is fit to be offered, the sanctity of the body takes hold of it and it is offered on the altar and therefore cannot be sold, here, where he consecrated it for a limited time, the sanctity of the body does not take effect - see Aruch HaShulchan 93:35).

she gave birth to two males, one shall be offered as a burnt offering and the second shall be sold for the needs of a burnt offering and its price is unconsecrated. The sanctity of a burnt offering took hold of both males that were born. However, he is obligated to bring only one, and therefore he sells one of them to someone who needs to bring a burnt offering, and the price of the sale is unconsecrated (Rashi, Temurah 24b).
tumtum. An animal whose sexual organs are hidden and it is not evident whether it is male or female.
and androgynos. That has both male and female sexual organs.

they are not consecrated and they are unconsecrated, as we have explained. For one who consecrates a tumtum or androgynos is like one who consecrates wood and stones, and they are unconsecrated for all purposes (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:10).
and similar to it. Animals that are disqualified from offering.
he vowed a small one and brought a large one. Of the kind that he vowed.
lamb. Up to one year of age.
ram. From one year and one month onward.
calf. Up to one year of age.
goat. Within its second year (above, 1:14).

and brought a peleges, there is doubt whether he fulfilled his vow or not. Male sheep up to one year are considered "lamb" and from one year and one month are considered "ram"; in the first thirty days of their second year they are called "peleges" and their halakhic definition is in doubt (see above, 1:14).

the turtledoves or from the young pigeons etc.. A bird burnt offering is from mature turtledoves or young pigeons. At the beginning of their yellowing they are no longer young but not yet mature, and they may not be offered (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:2), and if he brought them there is doubt whether he fulfilled his vow.
one who vows without specification. He vowed a certain kind of animal and did not specify its size.

and if in that place they are accustomed to call one of the kinds by the unspecified name etc.. If he vowed a certain offering (a burnt offering or peace offering) without specification, without specifying its kind, he brings the lesser kind that he might have meant, according to what is customarily called that in that place (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 13:6, Lechem Mishneh).
one peridah. A single bird.
he shall not bring the leanest of that kind. See also Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 7:1.

he shall bring an ox worth a maneh in that place, besides its libations. In his obligation he fixed the sum for the ox and did not include in this the libations that come with the offering (above, 2:1).
this ox is a burnt offering and it developed a blemish. And it must be sold and another animal bought with its proceeds and offered as a burnt offering.

if he wishes he may bring two with its proceeds, and even etc.. Since he undertook to bring a certain ox (as a freewill offering), after it developed a blemish his obligation was nullified (above, 14:5). However, he must bring a burnt offering from the proceeds of the ox, and therefore he may bring with the proceeds of the ox whatever burnt offering he wishes.
behold I take upon myself a burnt offering and he separated an ox and it was stolen, he may fulfill his obligation with a sheep. Since at the time of the vow he did not undertake to bring an ox.

this ox and its price are upon me as a burnt offering, it became fixed etc.. By saying this he undertook to bring specifically an ox (even if he brings another ox with the proceeds of this ox), and his obligation was fixed to bring another ox with the proceeds of this ox.
the largest of them is consecrated. Since one who consecrates something to the Temple treasury ordinarily consecrates generously (Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 108b).

if there were three, the largest of them is consecrated and we are concerned for the middle one. We are concerned that he intended to consecrate the middle one, since consecrating the middle one is also considered generous consecration relative to the small one (ibid.).

he shall wait for the middle one until it has a blemish and the sanctity will take effect on the large one alone. For after the middle one is disqualified and is not fit for offering, the large one alone becomes consecrated.
the ox among my oxen etc.. This language means the choicest ox in the herd, and therefore only the largest of them is consecrated.
he specified one of them and forgot. He consecrated a particular animal explicitly.
or his father said to him that one of them is consecrated. And did not tell him which animal was consecrated.

he consecrates the largest of them and afterward fulfills his obligation. For when he said explicitly of one of the animals that it is consecrated, he presumably consecrated the largest and choicest generously, and we are not concerned for the middle one.
and likewise one who vows a burnt offering etc.. A burnt offering does not come from females (above, 1:8), and therefore the doubt is only about males.
from the cattle and fixed his vow. He specified at the time of the vow an ox or a calf.
he shall bring an ox. For when one vows a small one he also fulfills with a large one (above, halakhah 1).
he fixed it among the sheep and forgot what he fixed. A small lamb or a ram.
he fixed it among the goats and forgot. Whether he vowed a kid or a goat.
a thanksgiving offering or peace offerings. They come from males and females (above, 1:11).
and he fixed his vow among the cattle and forgot in what he fixed it. He undertook to bring cattle and does not remember in what size (calf, bull) and whether male or female.
he shall bring a bull and a cow. And with this he also fulfills the obligation of the small ones (above, halakhah 1).
behold I take upon myself for the altar. This is interpreted as a vow to bring something that is entirely for the altar.
for there is nothing that is offered entirely to the altar as it is except. frankincense
. As explained below, halakhah 13. Whereas other things that are offered on the altar are not placed on the fire in their entirety (see Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 106b-107a).
he specified his vow and forgot what he specified. He said "I take upon myself for the altar" a particular thing, and forgot what he said.

he brings of every thing that is offered entirely to the altar. He brings of all the things that are offered to the altar and whose remainders are not eaten. In this case, since he mentioned what he must bring and did not say simply "for the altar," it is possible that he said something else and not necessarily frankincense.
and the meal offering of libations. Fine flour mixed with oil that comes with the offerings, and which one may vow on its own (above, 14:1).
behold I take upon myself a sela for the altar. I must bring to the altar something whose price is a sela.

for there is nothing that is offered for a sela to the altar except a lamb. For this is the ordinary price of a lamb (half the price of a ram, which the Torah fixed at two selas - Babylonian Talmud, Keritot 10b, and see Tosafot there).

he specified and forgot what he specified, he brings for a sela of everything etc.. When he undertook to bring a particular thing for the price of a sela and does not remember what he undertook, he brings of everything that can be offered, at the price of a sela (and he does not bring something that cannot be bought for a sela but only for a higher price, Rashi, Menachot 107b).
frankincense. For its identification see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 2:4.
than a handful. And its measure is no less than about two olives' bulk (above, 13:14).
behold I take upon myself wood. To bring for the arrangement of the fire on the altar.
their thickness like scrapers. The thickness of each log like the thickness of a stick used to remove the excess on a measuring vessel (see also Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 7:3).

and if he wished to bring the price of the wood, he brings. When he vowed wood he is not obligated to bring wood, but may bring its price to the Temple treasury so that wood will be bought with it (in the Temple there was a special chest into which they put the price of wood, Hilchot Shekalim 2:2).
the fires. The arranged fire on the altar.
like the remainders of meal offerings. Which are eaten by the priests after the burning of the handful (above, 12:9).
in wine that comes on its own. When he vowed to bring wine for the altar.
he puts salt on it. But on the wine of libations they do not put salt (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:11).
and pours all of it on the drains. Holes at the southwestern corner of the altar (above, 2:1).
from the money of second tithe. Redemption money of second tithe with which one buys food in Jerusalem and eats it there (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 2:1-2).
and anyone obligated in an offering etc.. But when he stipulated before the obligation that he would bring from tithe money, he may.
shall bring his offering only from unconsecrated produce. See also Hilchot Chagigah 2:8.
and its bread. The loaves that come with the thanksgiving offering (above, 9:17-22).

behold I take upon myself a thanksgiving offering from unconsecrated produce and its bread from tithe etc.. One who is obligated to bring a thanksgiving offering is obligated to bring its bread. Therefore he cannot stipulate regarding its loaves after he has already obligated himself for a thanksgiving offering from unconsecrated produce.
and if he brought everything from unconsecrated produce, he fulfilled. And this is the preferable way (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 7:5).

and he shall not bring its bread from wheat of second tithe but from the money of second tithe etc.. Although second tithe is separated from grain, one should not make the thanksgiving loaves from the wheat of second tithe, but they should be brought from second tithe money (wheat or loaves bought with the redemption money of second tithe).
like the animal, which is from the money of second tithe. For the animal itself cannot be second tithe.
for libations come only from unconsecrated produce, as we have explained. Above, 2:13.
oven. A large vessel under which they light wood, and dough is stuck to its sides for baking.

kuppach. A vessel in which wood is burned and on top of which there is a place for putting one pot (Hilchot Shabbat 3:7), and one can cook on it or bake inside it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 5:9).
baking on tiles. Baking by means of stones that were heated by fire (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
the Arabs' pit. A hole in the ground that they would plaster with clay and bake inside (Hilchot Kelim 16:6).
in the pan... in the frying pan. For their definition see above, 13:7.

what he brought he brought, and he did not fulfill his obligation. When he vowed and did not bring exactly what he vowed, he does not fulfill his vow and must bring a new meal offering. However, the meal offering he brought is valid.
this one to bring in the frying pan etc.. Since he specified that he would bring a certain fine flour in a certain manner, if he changed from what he said, the meal offering is invalid.
in one vessel... in two vessels. The meal offering in each vessel is considered a meal offering by itself, and from each vessel they burn one handful.
he did not fix them at the time of the vow. He vowed two isarons and did not specify in how many vessels he would bring them.
and he again brought them in one vessel. At the time of offering.
as you vowed and not as you separated. Only the obligation at the time of the vow obligates.

he offered them in two vessels, these are invalid. Although he did not say "these isarons," since when they told him that he had not brought as he vowed he did not answer them that he was bringing this meal offering as another freewill offering, it implies that he brought it for his vow, and it is invalid (Rik"v).
he offered them in one vessel, these are valid. And he fulfilled his vow.

he offered them in one vessel, these are like two meal offerings that were mixed. And their law is that if he can take a handful from each isaron separately they are valid, and if not they are invalid (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 11:29; and the same law applies above, halakhah 3, "these in two vessels and he brought in one vessel" - Rik"v).
from the five kinds of meal offering that come as a vow and freewill offering. Fine flour, pan, frying pan, loaves, and wafers (above, 12:4).

he shall bring two kinds of meal offerings of the five. Two meal offerings of two different kinds (and some explained that he may bring the two meal offerings of the same kind - see Rik"v, Kesef Mishneh and Radbaz).
two meal offerings of two kinds. One of each kind.
kinds of meal offering, he shall bring two kinds. One of each kind.
he fixed his vow in one of the kinds. He specified which kind he would bring.
of sixty isarons. About one hundred twenty-six liters.
for they cannot be mixed as one. It is impossible to mix properly such a large amount of fine flour and oil.
even though mixing is not indispensable, as we have explained. Above, 13:11.
anything fit for mixing etc.. Although it is valid when he did not mix, if it is impossible to mix it is invalid.

he specified his vow and forgot how many isarons he specified, he brings sixty isarons in one vessel. He vowed a certain amount and does not remember how much, he brings sixty (which is the largest amount that can be brought in one vessel).
he forgot how many isarons he specified and in which kind he fixed it. He vowed a particular meal offering in a particular amount, and does not remember what he vowed.

he fixed his vow and forgot how many isarons he vowed in how many vessels he vowed. He vowed a meal offering in a certain number of isarons and fixed that he would bring them in a number of vessels, and does not remember what he vowed.

a meal offering of barley... he is exempt. When he says "a meal offering of barley" in the construct form, he has undertaken to bring a kind of meal offering that is not offered, and his undertaking is meaningless and he is exempt.

behold I take upon myself a meal offering of barley... they ask him etc.. When he said "meal offering" as a separate word and then added "of barley," it is possible to understand his intention as having undertaken to bring a meal offering but adding a condition that it be of barley, and in this case one must clarify whether, had he known that one does not bring such a meal offering, he would have vowed differently or not.
he is obligated to offer in the way that they offer. A whole isaron, of wheat fine flour, with oil and frankincense.
an isaron and a half. And it is impossible to offer half isarons.
had I known, I would have vowed in the way that volunteers do. Two whole isarons.

and did not mention the name of a meal offering, he is exempt as if he had never vowed. In this case it is not a vow with a mistaken detail but an undertaking all of which is incorrect, and he is exempt even when he says that had he known that one does not offer this way he would have vowed in the way that volunteers do.
a thanksgiving offering without bread. A thanksgiving offering without thanksgiving loaves.
a sacrifice without libations. An offering without libations.
he is exempt. It is impossible to offer this way.
he is obligated to bring in the way that they offer. A thanksgiving offering with bread and a sacrifice with libations.
and the end of the offering he mentioned. When he mentioned the bread he also meant the offering.
he said, "behold I take upon myself bread to exempt the thanksgiving offering of so-and-so". See also above, 14:10.

and one does not volunteer a log of wine or two logs, for the libations do not have etc.. One who volunteers wine for the altar brings wine in the way that wine is brought for libations. In libations they bring three logs for a lamb, four for a ram, and six for a bull (above, 2:4). One should not bring one log, two logs, or five logs, since such measures do not exist among the libations.
and so forth forever. Any amount he volunteers is the sum of the libations of several offerings.
they say to him, complete six. Add one log and they will be offered as the libations of a bull.
for he fixed them for an offering. When he volunteered five, he obligated himself to offer all five for an offering, and the only way to offer them all together is by adding a log.
for they are not fit at all, neither they nor part of them. But when he vowed five, although he cannot offer all of them, some of them are fit, and therefore the vow takes effect.

and one does not volunteer or vow less than a log of oil, for you have no meal offering etc.. One who volunteers oil for the altar brings it in the way that oil is brought for mixing with meal offerings.

he specified his vow and forgot how many logs he vowed... for you have no day etc.. Although he does not remember how much he vowed, they did not obligate him to bring more than is brought with all the communal offerings on the day on which the community brings the greatest amount of offerings.

from the first day of a festival that fell on Shabbat etc.. The additional offering of the festival on the first day of Sukkot is thirteen bulls, two rams, and fourteen lambs. In addition, on this day they offer two lambs for the Shabbat additional offering and two lambs for the daily offering. The libations of each lamb are three logs of oil and wine, the libations of each ram four logs, and the libations of each bull six logs of oil and wine, and in total they brought one hundred forty logs.
as will be explained in the laws of daily and additional offerings. 10:3.
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
one who offers a sacrifice. He burns its limbs and fat on the altar (and the same applies to one who throws its blood and pours its libations, below, 19:3).

a fixed sin offering. A sin offering that always comes from an animal, in contrast to a burnt-or-sliding-scale offering that varies according to a person's financial situation (see Hilchot Shegagot 1:4).
even though he did not bring them up. To the altar.

and where did it warn about slaughter outside. The verse brought above, halakhah 3, teaches that the punishment of one who slaughters outside is karet. But we did not find a verse that prohibits slaughtering outside.

just as bringing up outside... so too an act that includes slaughter etc.. The verse compares the commandment of bringing up in the Temple to the commandment of slaughter in the Temple. From this we learn that just as there is a warning against the prohibition of bringing up outside the Temple, so too there is a warning against the prohibition of slaughter outside the Temple.
for the verse punishes only if it warned. There is no punishment of death or karet for an act that the Torah does not explicitly write not to do (see also Hilchot Mamrim 7:1).
one of the things forbidden for the altar. Animals that are disqualified for offering (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:11).
from the sin offerings that die. Sin offerings that cannot be offered and whose law is to die (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1).
lacking time in its body or in its owners. As explained in the adjacent halakhot.
within the seven days of birth. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:8.
and turtledoves whose time has not yet come. Young turtledoves (ibid., halakhah 2).

it and its offspring, one of which was slaughtered today. It is forbidden to slaughter an animal and its offspring on the same day (Hilchot Shechitah 12:1-3). Therefore when one of them is slaughtered, the other is disqualified for offering on that day.

the zav, the zavah, and the woman who gave birth who slaughtered their sin offerings... and likewise a leper. After these impure persons are purified from their impurity, they must count days of purity, and afterward offer offerings to complete the process of their atonement (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:4-5, 4:1).
they became fit. They became suitable.
if they slaughtered their burnt offerings. Which they bring with the sin offering at the end of their purification.
for the burnt offering is a gift. A present, an additional appeasement.

a nazirite who slaughtered etc.. At the end of the nazirite period the nazirite brings a sin offering, burnt offering, and peace offering (above, 1:6). The sin offering is the main offering he is required to bring, and therefore before the end of the nazirite period he is considered lacking time (although if he brings only a burnt offering or peace offering, immediately after bringing them he may complete the laws of his nazirite status - Lechem Mishneh, Nezirut 8:10).
a suspensive guilt offering. Above, 1:6.

and a bird sin offering that comes for a doubt. When he is in doubt whether he is obligated in a bird sin offering (such as a doubtful woman who gave birth and a doubtful zavah), he brings a bird and offers it as a sin offering out of doubt (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 7:10).

for the prohibition was not fixed. There is no certainty that he is obligated in an offering, and it is possible that it is not fit to be offered inside (if it becomes known that he did not sin), and therefore he is exempt (see Mirkevet HaMishneh).

a leper's guilt offering that he slaughtered outside not for its own sake. Not for the sake of a guilt offering. And the offering is valid and is offered on the altar, but it does not count for the leper for his obligation and he must bring another guilt offering (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 5:2); and since it does not count for the leper for his obligation, he is liable even if he slaughtered it during the days of his counting (see above, halakhah 9), for in this way it is valid even before its time (Babylonian Talmud, Zevachim 114b).

since not for its own sake is fit inside and valid, as will be explained. For all offerings except a sin offering and a Passover offering are valid when done not for their own sake (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:1).
the two goats of Yom Kippur. One of them is offered in the Temple and the second is sent to Azazel, after confession is made over it in the courtyard.

since they are fit to come before the Lord for confession. Although the sent goat is not offered in the Temple, since confession is made over it in the courtyard it is considered fit to come before the Lord, and one is liable for slaughtering it outside.
and if after he confessed, he is exempt for the sent one. See also below, 19:7.
as we have explained. Above, 5:5, that it is forbidden to offer peace offerings before the opening of the doors, and if they were slaughtered they are invalid.

on the other days of the year, whether for its own sake or not for its own sake, he is liable. When he slaughtered a Passover offering on other days of the year, its law is that of a peace offering. Therefore whether he slaughtered for the sake of a Passover offering or for the sake of another offering, the offering is valid (for peace offerings slaughtered not for their own sake are valid - Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:1), and one is liable for slaughtering it outside. However, if he slaughtered the Passover offering outside in its proper time not for its own sake, he is exempt, for a Passover offering slaughtered not for its own sake is invalid (Birkat Avraham, sec. 7, Kesef Mishneh; and see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:11).
whose fetus is consecrated for the altar. When he consecrated only the fetus for an offering (see above, 15:8).
it is forbidden to slaughter it outside. For the slaughter of the mother is considered the slaughter of the fetus (Radbaz).
because it is not fit to come before the Lord. For the mother is an unconsecrated animal and the fetus has not yet been born.

and from when did they place it in his possession in order to make him liable for karet etc.. Before the owner despairs, the animal still belongs to the owner (Hilchot Genevah 5:2-3), and the thief cannot consecrate it and offer it (ibid. 2:6). However, if he consecrated the animal before despair and slaughtered it outside after despair, since at the time of slaughter it was already in his possession, they considered it retroactively his from the time of consecration and he is liable for karet for slaughtering it (Mirkevet HaMishneh, Ma'aseh LaMelech; and see further Hilchot Gezelah 2:8).
until the entire animal is in the Temple. Compare Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:14.
one who slaughters on the roof of the Sanctuary, even though it is not fit for slaughter at all. Above, 5:4.
two who held a knife and slaughtered outside are exempt. In contrast to two who offered up outside, who are liable (below, 19:12).
even though he did not intend to slaughter these consecrated animals to the Lord. But he slaughtered for eating or for another purpose.
he is liable. Unlike above, where he is liable only if he offered it up for the sake of the Lord (below 19:1).
since slaughtering at night is valid outside. Therefore, although the slaughter of sacrificial animals in the Temple is valid only by day, one who slaughters at night outside is liable.
but if he slaughtered inside at night and offered it up outside, he is exempt. Both for the slaughter and for the offering up.
for there is no valid slaughter at night in the Temple. Above 4:1.

likewise, if he received the blood in a non-sacred vessel inside and sprinkled it outside, he is exempt. For blood received in a non-sacred vessel is invalid for sprinkling (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:24). But if he slaughtered outside and received the blood in a non-sacred vessel and sprinkled the blood outside, he is liable for the sprinkling as well (Babylonian Talmud, Zevachim 111b).

likewise, one who nips a bird's neck outside is exempt, and if he offered it up he is exempt. Nipping a bird is valid only for an offering and in the Temple. A bird nipped outside the Temple is considered a carcass and is invalid for offering, and one is not liable for its slaughter or for offering it up outside.

if he slaughtered it inside and offered it up outside, he is exempt, etc.. Slaughtering a bird in the Temple is considered like strangling or tearing the neck (above 6:23), and it is invalid for offering.
the altar. A structure of stones.

and he is not liable until he offers it up for the Name. That he offers the sacrifice for the sake of the Lord (unlike the slaughterer, who is liable even if he slaughtered for a layman, above 18:16).
to the fires. Burning on the fire.
or to the altar. Sprinkling, dashing, and pouring of libations.
the emurin (portions burned on the altar). Of offerings that are eaten.
the handful or the frankincense. Of the meal offerings.
incense. That which is fit for burning on the inner altar.
the meal offering of priests or the meal offering of libations. These are burned entirely on the altar.
one who pours three logs of wine. The smallest measure of libations (above 2:4).

three logs of water. The measure of water that was poured on the altar on the festival of Sukkot (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 10:7), and the case here is where he poured it on Sukkot (Kesef Mishneh; and see Radbaz).
the remainder of the blood. The blood of the offering left over after the blood was applied to the altar, which is poured on the base (above 5:10-11).
even the remainder of the inner blood. Of the bulls and goats that are burned.
for the sprinkling of the remainder of the blood is a remainder of the commandment. And is not part of the essential commandment.
on the festival. Sukkot.
for all of these are fit for eating, not for the fires. And it is forbidden to burn them on the altar (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:5).
for the handful is not distinct and separate. Before the taking of the handful, there is no specific, defined part of the meal offering that is the handful.

if he took the handful, then returned the handful into it, and offered all of it outside, he is liable. Since the handful was separate and distinct, it is considered on its own, and one is liable for burning it.
one who pours, mixes, breaks into pieces, salts, waves, and brings near. The meal offerings (for an explanation of these acts see above 12:6, 13:5-8).
and one who arranges the table. The showbread or the dishes of frankincense that are on it.
and one who trims the lamps. Prepares the lamps of the menorah for lighting.
and one who takes the handful. From a meal offering.
for none of these is the completion of the service. And there is further service after it that completes and concludes it (see also Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 9:5).

a red heifer that he burned outside its place of burning. The heifer was burned at a place specially prepared for it on the Mount of Anointing. When it was burned outside this place it is invalid, like offerings that were offered outside the Temple court (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 14:1).
the scapegoat that he offered outside. Instead of sending it to Azazel in the wilderness.
after he confessed over it. But before the confession, one is liable for it (above 18:11).

that were disqualified in the Temple... is liable. Offerings that were valid when brought to the Temple and were disqualified afterward, during or after the slaughter (as distinct from those unfit for the altar from the outset, as above 18:6).
for all of them are burned, as will be explained in Hilchot Pesulei Kodashim. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:1.
and these were done for the Lord. And were disqualified afterward.
if any of that which is offered is missing inside. For example, if it was lost or burned.
and the burnt offering. The limbs of the burnt offering.
a burnt offering and its emurin combine to make an olive's bulk. For with a burnt offering the flesh is burned as well, not only the emurin.

for Scripture distinguished between one who offers up and one who performs. The verse treats the prohibition of offering up and the prohibition of performing the other acts of the sacrifice separately.

if he offered up a deficient limb he is exempt. If he offered up an olive's bulk from a limb part of which was lost. But if the whole limb exists, he is liable even if he offered up only an olive's bulk from it (as above, halakhah 8 - Mishneh Lamelech; and see Likkutei Halakhot, Zevachim 108b, who explained otherwise).
two who held a limb and offered it up outside are liable. Unlike slaughter (above 18:16).
one who sprinkles some of the applications outside is liable. He sprinkled only part of the blood of the sacrifice and not all the sprinklings that must be sprinkled for that sacrifice.
for all of it is still fit to be offered inside. For they had not yet sprinkled the blood on the altar.
and if he applied from it inside. All the applications.
because they are remainders. Which are not essential, and one is exempt for them (above, halakhah 4).
but if he received it in two cups. The blood in both of them is valid for sprinkling (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 2:21).
one outside and one inside. He applied from the first cup outside before he sprinkled inside.

or one inside and one outside, he is liable. For in this case the blood in the second cup is not considered remainders. Even though the blood in it is no longer fit for sprinkling (since the sacrifice's blood was already applied to the altar from the first cup), one is liable for sprinkling it, just as one is liable for offering sacrifices that were disqualified in the sacred precincts (Mirkevet HaMishneh, Even HaEzel).
the handful and the frankincense of a meal offering. They burn both of them (above 13:12).

and likewise the two dishes of frankincense of the showbread. On the table beside the showbread were two vessels containing frankincense. On the Sabbath, when the showbread was removed from the table, the frankincense was burned on the altar (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 5:5).
because it is fit to be offered inside. A sacrifice that was slaughtered outside is fit, even nowadays, to be offered inside.
for it is permitted to offer even though there is no House there... as we have explained. Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:15.
that they offer on a private altar that they build. On a built altar, and not on a rock or stone, which are not considered an altar (above, halakhah 1).
and it is forbidden to assist them or to act as their agent. To help them offer and to offer on their behalf.
